options.content: All the metals will give out photo electrons with same kinetic energies.

en.explanation:
The Einstein's photoelectric equation states that the energy of incident photons to the work function of the metal and the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

Where is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons, is the energy of the incident photon (where h is Planck's constant and is frequency) and is the work function of the metal, which is the minimum energy required to eject an electron.

The work function can also be expressed in terms of the threshold frequency , which is the minimum frequency required for photoelectric emission:

The stopping potential ( ) is the negative potential applied to stop the most energetic photoelectrons. The work done by this potential equals the maximum kinetic energy:

Substituting this into the photoelectric equation:

The equation is in the form of a straight line .

The slope constant for all metals, which is why the lines are parallel.

X -intercept represents the threshold frequency , where . At this frequency, the incident energy exactly equals the work function .

From the graph, we can identify the threshold frequencies for each metal:

Now, considering incident radiation of the same wavelength ( ).

Since energy , the incident energy is the same for all three metals.

Substituting this into the energy equation:

Since is constant, the metal with the smallest work function ( ) will result in the greatest kinetic energy ( ).

As metal has the lowest threshold frequency and thus the lowest work function, it will emit electrons with the greatest kinetic energy.
